claims.text: Adding a small amount of dysprosium to a magnetic high-entropy alloy will increase its coercive field.
The baseline magnetic high-entropy alloy contains no rare-earth elements.
Dysprosium addition will increase magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Dysprosium will promote domain-wall pinning at grain boundaries.
Increased magnetocrystalline anisotropy will make magnetization reversal more difficult.
Domain-wall pinning at grain boundaries will make magnetization reversal more difficult.
More difficult magnetization reversal will produce a higher coercive field.
At room temperature after standard processing, the dysprosium-containing alloy will have a higher coercive field than a matched alloy without dysprosium.
The coercivity-increasing effect should hold when the dysprosium content is below its solubility limit.
The coercivity-increasing effect should hold when the alloy is not subjected to high temperatures.
The coercivity-increasing effect should hold when the alloy is not subjected to external stresses.
A vibrating sample magnetometer can be used to compare coercive fields and magnetization curves of dysprosium-containing and dysprosium-free samples.
Failure of the dysprosium-containing alloy to show a significantly higher coercive field than the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
